questions.prompt: What topology is the amplifier?
questions.correct: Three-op-amp instrumentation amp with AC-coupled inputs (handout Fig. 2)
distractors: Unity-gain followers into a difference amp that carries all of the gain
Two-op-amp instrumentation amp with a DC servo integrator on its output
Single difference amplifier fed straight from the electrodes via 10 kΩ
questions.explanation: 2): A1 and A2 as a gain stage sharing R1–C1, then A3 as a difference amplifier. The board is Fig. 2 from the handout: AC-coupled inputs (C_c into R_c), stage 1 = A1/A2 non-inverting amps with R2 feedback and R1–C1 between their inverting inputs, stage 2 = A3 difference amp with R3/R4 and C4. The follower version with all gain in stage 2 was Rev C, which was never built.
questions.modelAnswer: A three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier with AC-coupled inputs (the handout's Fig.
questions.sayIt: Three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier with AC-coupled inputs. Stage 1 gain 10.7, stage 2 gain 12.1, total 130 or 42.3 dB.

questions.prompt: What is the designed mid-band differential gain?
questions.explanation: 42.3 dB. A0 = α·G1·G2 = 0.9985 × 10.71 × 12.14 = 129.8 → 42.27 dB. 140 was the 12 Oct design with R3 = 52 kΩ; 136 was Rev C; 134.7 (42.59 dB) is what was measured on ±15 V, 0.3 dB high from resistor tolerance.

questions.prompt: Why was a total gain of about 130 chosen?
questions.correct: 100–200 is needed for ≈2 V pk from a 10–20 mV QRS; 130 sits mid-window
distractors: It is the most gain that keeps the worst-case 7.7 V offset inside 3–12 V
It is where OP27 current noise and resistor noise are equal at the output
It gives exactly 60 dB of CMRR with 1 % resistors in stage 2
questions.explanation: 2 V / 20 mV = 100 and 2 V / 10 mV = 200. 130 sits in that window and 42.3 dB is 2.3 dB above the 40 dB floor. The 7.7 V worst-case offset does not fit the single-supply window at any useful gain.
questions.modelAnswer: The Brief wants ≈2 V pk out for a 10–20 mV pk QRS, so gain must be 100–200; 130 gives 1.3–2.6 V pk and sits inside the 40–54 dB gain spec.
questions.sayIt: 2 V out from 10–20 mV in needs 100 to 200. 130 gives 1.3 to 2.6 V and is inside 40–54 dB.

questions.prompt: Explain the stage-1 gain. What is the formula and value?
questions.explanation: Each inverting input follows its + input, so V2 − V1 appears across R1 (C1 shorted at signal frequencies). That current i = (V2−V1)/R1 flows through both R2s, so V_O2 − V_O1 = (V2 − V1)(1 + 2R2/R1). Both R2s count, hence the 2.
questions.sayIt: Stage 1 has gain 10.7 for signals and gain 1 at DC and for common-mode.

questions.prompt: Explain the stage-2 gain. What is the formula and value?
questions.explanation: With matched arms Vo = (Z4/R3)(V_O2 − V_O1), and at mid-band Z4 = R4, so G2 = R4/R3 = 12.14. 13.14 is the noise gain 1 + G2 (sets A3's bandwidth), and 13.08 used the old 52 kΩ R3 from the 12 Oct page.
questions.sayIt: Stage 2 is Z4 over R3 times the difference: 12.1 at mid-band.

questions.prompt: Why put gain in stage 1 at all instead of using followers and all 130 in stage 2?
questions.correct: Stage 1 passes common-mode at 1, so its gain multiplies the CMRR
distractors: The OP27 can't hold a closed-loop gain of 130 out to 150 Hz
Stage-1 gain keeps the A1/A2 outputs away from their swing limits
Gain in stage 1 divides the output DC offset down by G1
questions.explanation: Stage 1 lifts the wanted signal 10.7× above the common-mode before the difference amp has to separate them. It also follows the Brief's recommendation. The OP27 at gain 130 would still have ~60 kHz bandwidth, and stage-1 outputs only swing ±0.1 V, so those are not the reasons.
questions.modelAnswer: Stage 1 amplifies differential signals by G1 but passes common-mode at exactly 1, so its gain multiplies the CMRR (CMRR_R = G1(1 + G2)/4t).
questions.sayIt: Stage 1 amplifies differential signals and passes common-mode at 1, so its gain multiplies CMRR.

questions.prompt: What limits how much gain stage 1 can take?
questions.correct: The 10 µF limit on C1 forces R1 high, so more G1 needs a bigger R2
distractors: The OP27 input common-mode range shrinks as stage-1 gain rises
Above G1 ≈ 11 the 30 mV p-p noise limit is always exceeded
The A1/A2 outputs would clip, since they carry G1 × electrode DC
questions.explanation: R1 = 1/(2π f C1). With C1 ≤ 10 µF and f ≈ 23 mHz, R1 ≈ 680 kΩ. G1 = 1 + 2R2/R1 then needs R2 in megohms; 3.3 MΩ already gives the stray-C slope above 20 Hz and dominates the noise.
questions.modelAnswer: C1 is capped at 10 µF (largest stock part), which forces R1 up to 680 kΩ for a 23 mHz corner; more G1 then needs a bigger R2, which raises offset, noise and the stray-capacitance CMRR error.

questions.prompt: Why was Rev C (followers in stage 1, ×136 in stage 2) not used?
questions.correct: Offset would be multiplied by 136, and CMRR loses the G1 multiplier
distractors: It fails the ±20° phase spec at 0.5 Hz with followers in stage 1
It needs a fourth op-amp, breaking the stock-parts-only rule
Stage 2 alone cannot reach 40 dB with stock resistor values
questions.explanation: Rev C removed the 3.3 MΩ nodes (and the stray-C error) but its DC gain on offset was 136 with no C1 to block it, and stage 1 at unity means CMRR gets no G1 multiplier. Its phase was +1.8°/−8.2°, which passes, and it used stock parts.
questions.modelAnswer: It multiplies the stage-1 DC offset difference by 136 instead of 12 (up to ~9.5 V) and gives up the CMRR benefit of stage-1 gain.
questions.sayIt: It removes the high-impedance nodes but multiplies DC offset by 136 and gives up the CMRR benefit of stage-1 gain.

questions.prompt: At 15 Hz with the fixture's V_id ≈ 19 mV pk (9.5 mV on each input), what is at each stage-1 output?
questions.correct: ≈102 mV pk each, 203 mV pk differential
distractors: ≈9.5 mV pk each; stage 1 is a follower at 15 Hz
≈1.02 V pk each, 2.03 V pk differential
≈203 mV pk each, 406 mV pk differential
questions.explanation: Each output is G1 × its own input: 10.71 × 9.5 mV ≈ 102 mV, opposite in phase, so V_O2 − V_O1 ≈ 203 mV. Stage 2 then gives 12.14 × 203 mV ≈ 2.47 V pk.
questions.modelAnswer: About 102 mV pk each (10.71 × 9.5 mV), 203 mV pk differential.
questions.sayIt: 9.5 mV at each input, 102 mV at each stage-1 output, 203 mV differential, 2.5 V at Vo.

questions.prompt: Which node limits the signal headroom?
questions.correct: Vo; the stage-1 outputs only swing about ±0.1 V
distractors: The stage-1 outputs, which carry G1 × electrode DC
A3's + pin, which sits at 0.924 × V_O2
The A1/A2 + inputs, because of the 68 mV bias drop
questions.explanation: Stage 1 only has to deliver ~102 mV pk. All the swing (2.6 V pk for a 20 mV QRS) plus the output offset lands on Vo, which is why the single-supply headroom check is done at Vo against the 3–12 V window.
questions.modelAnswer: Vo, the A3 output; the stage-1 outputs only swing about ±0.1 V.

questions.prompt: The measured gain was 42.59 dB against 42.27 dB designed. What explains the 0.3 dB?
questions.correct: Resistor tolerance: a constant gain error at every frequency
distractors: Finite OP27 gain-bandwidth lifting the mid-band
The 0.15 % input-network loss being smaller than modelled
Coupling-capacitor tolerance shifting the mid-band level
questions.explanation: Gain depends only on R1, R2, R3, R4 (a 10 % error in one moves gain by 0.75–0.83 dB). A constant offset across the whole sweep means the corners are right and only the mid-band ratio is off. Capacitors only move corners; the OP27 adds 0.0013 % gain error.
questions.modelAnswer: Resistor tolerance on R1–R4: the error is a constant 0.3–0.5 dB at every frequency, so it is a pure gain error, not a corner error.

questions.prompt: Is the amplifier inverting or non-inverting with respect to V2?
questions.correct: Non-inverting: Vo is in phase with V2 (−0.7° at 15 Hz)
distractors: Inverting: Vo is 180° from V2
Inverting at low frequency, non-inverting above 5 Hz
It depends on which input the fixture's inverter drives
questions.explanation: V2 drives A2's + input, V_O2 drives A3's + input through R3_a, so the path is non-inverting. The −0.7° at 15 Hz is the low-pass lag (−0.82°) minus a little high-pass lead (+0.09°).

questions.prompt: What is the job of the coupling capacitors C_ca and C_cb (10 µF)?
questions.correct: Block electrode half-cell DC and set the input high-pass
distractors: Filter out 50 Hz mains interference before it reaches stage 1
Set the 1054 Hz low-pass corner together with R_c
Provide the DC bias-current path into the op-amp + inputs
questions.explanation: Electrodes carry hundreds of mV of DC. C_c blocks it so it is never amplified. With R_c it forms a high-pass at 2.3 mHz. The bias path is R_c's job; the low-pass is R4–C4.
questions.modelAnswer: Block the electrodes' DC half-cell potential and set the input high-pass; on one supply they also let the amplifier side sit at 7.5 V while the source side is at 0 V.

questions.prompt: What is the job of R_ca and R_cb (6.8 MΩ)?
questions.correct: Give the + pins a DC bias path and set their DC level
distractors: Set the stage-1 differential gain together with R1
Match the electrode impedance for maximum power transfer
Form the 1054 Hz low-pass together with C_c
questions.explanation: After C_c there is no DC path to the op-amp + pin except R_c. Without it the bias current would charge C_c until the input saturated. It is returned to 0 V (dual) or VREF (single), so the pin sits at VREF − I_b·R_c ≈ 7.43 V.
questions.modelAnswer: Give the + inputs a DC path for their bias current, set their DC level, and set the input impedance.

questions.prompt: What is the input network's time constant and corner?
questions.explanation: H_in(s) = sR_cC_c / (1 + s(R_s + R_c)C_c). Pole at 1/(2π·68.1 s) = 2.34 mHz. 72.8 s is the stage-1 zero that cancels this pole; 6.8 s is the R1C1 pole that is the real lower corner; 3.3 s was the old 0.33 µF / 10 MΩ network.
questions.modelAnswer: τ = (R_s + R_c)C_c = 6.81 MΩ × 10 µF = 68.1 s, corner 2.34 mHz.
questions.sayIt: 10 µF into 6.8 MΩ is a 68 second high-pass at 2.3 millihertz.

questions.prompt: Why is R_c 6.8 MΩ?
questions.correct: 69.8 dB electrode-mismatch CMRR, and 68 s with 10 µF for cancellation
distractors: It equals 2 × R2, which balances the A1/A2 bias-current drops
It is the largest stock resistor, giving maximum input impedance
With C1 it sets the 23 mHz lower corner of the whole amplifier
questions.explanation: R_c forms a divider with each electrode impedance; mismatched electrodes then convert common-mode to differential, and the error scales as R_s/R_c. 10 MΩ would give 73.2 dB but τ = 100 s and more offset (I_b·R_c). 6.8 MΩ × 10 µF = 68 s ≈ 72.8 s.
questions.modelAnswer: Electrode-mismatch CMRR R_c/[2R_s(Δ_c + Δ_s)] gives 69.8 dB; with 10 µF it gives 68 s to meet the pole-zero condition; and it has 32 % less bias-current offset than 10 MΩ.
questions.sayIt: Electrode mismatch: CMRR = R_c over 2 R_s (Δ_c + Δ_s) = 69.8 dB. And 6.8 MΩ × 10 µF matches the cancellation condition.

questions.prompt: What electrode-mismatch CMRR does R_c = 6.8 MΩ give with 10 kΩ sources, 10 % electrode and 1 % resistor mismatch?
questions.explanation: 69.8 dB. CMRR_e = Z_c / [2 Z_s (Δ_c + Δ_s)]. 73.2 dB is the 10 MΩ version, 70.9 dB is the stage-2 resistor term, and 64.3 dB is those two combined (in real use). This term never appears on the bench because the Brief's CMRR test drives both inputs directly.

questions.prompt: How much signal does the input network lose in the passband?
questions.correct: About 0.15 % (−0.013 dB), from the R_s–R_c divider
distractors: About 3 dB at 0.5 Hz, from the high-pass corner
About 10 %, from the 10 kΩ source impedance
None; a high-pass has unity gain in its passband
questions.explanation: Above ~0.02 Hz the capacitor is a short, leaving the R_s–R_c divider. That is the α = 0.9985 in A0 = α·G1·G2.

questions.prompt: Why do the test scripts wait 300 s before measuring?
questions.correct: The input nodes settle with τ = 68 s; 5τ ≈ 340 s
distractors: The OP27 bias current drifts for ~5 minutes after power-up
C_ref needs 300 s to charge VREF to 7.5 V
The generator's DC offset takes 300 s to stabilise
questions.explanation: After any disturbance the + pin returns to VREF − I_b·R_c through the 68 s time constant. VREF itself settles in 5 × 34 ms = 0.17 s.
questions.modelAnswer: The input nodes settle with τ = 68 s; 1 % settling takes about 5τ ≈ 340 s.

questions.prompt: Why was the input network changed from 0.33 µF / 10 MΩ to 10 µF / 6.8 MΩ between 30 Oct and 2 Nov?
questions.correct: To meet C_cR_c ≈ C1(R1 + 2R2), which also fixed 0.5 Hz CMRR
distractors: To reduce the thermal noise that the 10 MΩ R_c was contributing
The 0.33 µF parts leaked and slowly drifted the input DC levels
To move the lower −3 dB corner up to exactly 0.5 Hz
questions.explanation: With τ = 3.3 s the input pole sat far from the stage-1 zero, leaving a shelf and +38° at 0.1 Hz. Time-constant CMRR is |1 + jωτ|/δ; at 0.5 Hz that factor went from 10.4 to 214, which is the 55 → 76 dB jump.
questions.modelAnswer: To meet the Brief's pole-zero condition C_cR_c ≈ C1(R1 + 2R2) (3.3 s → 68 s vs 72.8 s), which also lifted 0.5 Hz CMRR from 55 dB to 76 dB.

questions.prompt: What DC voltage drop does the OP27 bias current produce across R_c?
questions.correct: ≈68 mV typical (10 nA × 6.8 MΩ)
distractors: None, because C_c blocks all DC
questions.explanation: C_c blocks source DC but not the bias current, which flows through R_c. On one supply that puts the + pins at 7.5 − 0.068 ≈ 7.43 V.
questions.modelAnswer: About 68 mV typical (10 nA × 6.8 MΩ), up to 272 mV at the 40 nA maximum.

questions.prompt: Why is C_c 10 µF rather than larger?
questions.correct: It is the largest capacitor the Brief's parts list allows
distractors: Anything larger would push the high-pass corner above 0.5 Hz
Anything larger would also cancel the stage-1 R1C1 pole
10 µF with 6.8 MΩ makes the input impedance exactly 10 MΩ
questions.explanation: The Brief allows capacitors up to 10 µF. The largest C_c lets R_c be as small as possible (less offset) for a given τ. The same limit is why C1 is 10 µF and R1 is 680 kΩ.
questions.modelAnswer: 10 µF is the largest capacitor allowed by the Brief's materials list (stock parts only).

questions.prompt: What is C1 for?
questions.correct: Opens R1 at DC so stage-1 DC gain is 1, not 10.7
distractors: Sets the 1054 Hz low-pass corner together with R1
Blocks electrode DC from reaching the op-amp inputs
Cancels the input-network pole on its own, without R2
questions.explanation: At DC, Z1 = R1 + 1/(sC1) is infinite, so G1 = 1 and A1/A2 are followers. Only stage 2's 12.14 multiplies the offset difference. Without C1 the offset would see the full 130.
questions.modelAnswer: It opens the R1 branch at DC so stage-1 DC gain is 1; the A1/A2 offset difference is then multiplied by 12, not 130.
questions.sayIt: It makes stage-1 gain 1 at DC, so the offset difference is multiplied by 12, not 130.

questions.prompt: What is stage 1's common-mode gain?
questions.correct: Exactly 1, whatever the resistor values
distractors: 10.71, the same as the differential gain
1 + R2/R1, about 5.9
Zero, since stage 1 rejects common-mode
questions.explanation: If V1 = V2, both inverting inputs sit at the same voltage, so no current flows in R1–C1, none flows in R2, and each output equals its input. This is why the common-mode is not amplified and CMRR gets the G1 multiplier.

questions.prompt: Which expression is stage 1's differential transfer function G1(s)?
questions.explanation: G1 = 1 + 2R2/Z1 with Z1 = R1 + 1/(sC1) = (1 + sR1C1)/(sC1). So G1 = 1 + 2R2·sC1/(1 + sR1C1) = [1 + s(R1 + 2R2)C1]/(1 + sR1C1). DC gain 1, high-frequency gain (R1 + 2R2)/R1 = 10.71: a lead network.

questions.prompt: Where are stage 1's pole and zero?
questions.correct: Pole 23.4 mHz (R1C1); zero 2.19 mHz ((R1 + 2R2)C1)
distractors: Pole 2.19 mHz ((R1 + 2R2)C1); zero 23.4 mHz (R1C1)
Pole 23.4 mHz (R1C1); zero at the origin (C1)
Pole 1054 Hz (R4C4); zero 23.4 mHz (R1C1)
questions.explanation: τ_p = 680 k × 10 µ = 6.8 s → 23.4 mHz. τ_z = 7.28 M × 10 µ = 72.8 s → 2.19 mHz. The zero sits below the pole by exactly G1 (f_p/f_z = 10.71), which is the step up in gain.

questions.prompt: What is the pole-zero cancellation condition and how close is the build?
distractors: R1C1 = C_cR_c: 6.8 s vs 68.0 s, 90 % apart
C1R2 = C_cR_c: 33 s vs 68.0 s, 51 % apart
R1C1 = R4C4: 6.8 s vs 151 µs
questions.explanation: The stage-1 zero at −1/τ_z must land on the input pole at −1/τ_in. The Brief states it as C1(R1 + 2R2) = C_cR_c. The leftover pole-zero pair is 0.15 mHz apart near 2.3 mHz and adds 0.09° at 0.1 Hz.
questions.modelAnswer: C1(R1 + 2R2) = C_cR_c: 72.8 s against 68.0 s, 7 % apart.

questions.prompt: After pole-zero cancellation, what sets the amplifier's lower −3 dB corner?
questions.correct: R1C1 alone: 23.4 mHz
distractors: R_cC_c alone: 2.34 mHz
The stage-1 zero: 2.19 mHz
questions.explanation: The input pole (cut below 2.34 mHz) and stage-1 zero (boost below 2.19 mHz) undo each other, leaving R1C1. The exact model gives 23.6 mHz at −3 dB.
questions.modelAnswer: Stage 1's pole alone: 1/(2πR1C1) = 23.4 mHz.
questions.sayIt: Its zero at 2.2 millihertz cancels the input pole, so the only high-pass corner left is 1 over 2π R1 C1, 23 millihertz.

questions.prompt: If the input pole and stage-1 zero were far apart (as with the old 0.33 µF network), what would you see?
questions.correct: A shelf in the low-frequency gain and extra lead at 0.5 Hz
distractors: Ringing in the step response near the lower corner
A notch in the gain response close to 50 Hz
Higher mid-band gain, by roughly the pole-zero ratio
questions.explanation: Uncancelled, the response has two separate high-pass corners with a step between them. On 30 Oct the 3.3 s network gave +41° at 0.1 Hz against +14.9° after the change.

questions.prompt: Why is R1 680 kΩ?
questions.correct: C1 is capped at 10 µF, so R1 must be ≈680 kΩ for 23 mHz
distractors: It matches R4 so both stages share a time constant
It gives the lowest thermal noise for the stage
It sets the input impedance together with R_c
questions.explanation: R1C1 is the only low-frequency corner after cancellation. The 10 µF ceiling on C1 forces R1 high. R1 thermal noise is actually the second-largest noise source.
questions.modelAnswer: With C1 capped at 10 µF, R1 = 1/(2π · 23 mHz · 10 µF) ≈ 680 kΩ for the lower corner, and it sets G1 with R2.

questions.prompt: How was R2 = 3.3 MΩ chosen?
questions.correct: From the gain: R2 = (G1 − 1)R1/2 ≈ 3.3 MΩ
distractors: Set to R_c/2 so the bias-current drops cancel
Set by the stray-capacitance limit at the stage-1 nodes
Chosen for minimum current-noise contribution
questions.explanation: (10.71 − 1) × 680 k / 2 = 3.3 MΩ. Larger R2 raises offset (I_os·R2), noise (i_n·R2 dominates) and the stray-capacitance CMRR slope.
questions.modelAnswer: From the gain: R2 = (G1 − 1)R1/2 for G1 ≈ 10.7 with R1 = 680 kΩ; it also sets the stage-1 zero τ_z = C1(R1 + 2R2) = 72.8 s.

questions.prompt: What would a larger R2 cost?
questions.correct: More offset, more noise and a worse stray-C CMRR slope
distractors: Lower input impedance seen by the electrodes, so more loading
A higher low-pass corner and therefore less phase lag at 150 Hz
Higher common-mode gain through stage 1
questions.explanation: i_n × R2 is the largest noise term (174 nV/√Hz referred to input). CMRR_stray = G1/(ωR2ΔC), so it worsens with R2. Offset includes I_b(R2 − R_c) and (I_os/2)(R2 + R_c).
questions.modelAnswer: More DC offset, more noise (OP27 current noise × R2) and a steeper stray-capacitance CMRR error.

questions.prompt: What is the closed-loop bandwidth of A1 and A2?
distractors: 8 MHz / 130 ≈ 62 kHz
questions.explanation: OP27 GBW ≈ 8 MHz; noise gain of each stage-1 amp at signal frequencies is G1. 609 kHz is A3 (noise gain 1 + G2). These poles are three decades above the low-pass and add 0.03° at 150 Hz.

questions.prompt: Why is the stage-1 lead network's pole-zero spacing exactly the stage-1 gain?
questions.correct: τ_z/τ_p = (R1 + 2R2)/R1, which is G1
distractors: C1 equals C_c, so the time constants scale together
The zero is at the origin, so the spacing is G1
The OP27 GBW sets both the pole and the zero
questions.explanation: A lead network steps from DC gain 1 to HF gain τ_z/τ_p. Here that ratio is 72.8/6.8 = 10.71.

questions.prompt: What is the upper (low-pass) cutoff and what sets it?
distractors: GBW/(1 + G2) ≈ 609 kHz
questions.explanation: Z4 = R4 ∥ 1/(sC4) gives Vo = (R4/R3)/(1 + sR4C4) × (V_O2 − V_O1). τ_4 = 151 µs, pole at −6624 rad/s = 1054 Hz. 6624 is the rad/s figure; divide by 2π.
questions.sayIt: Rolling off at 1 over 2π R4 C4, about 1 kilohertz, which costs 8 degrees at 150 hertz.

questions.prompt: Why is C4 222 pF?
questions.correct: Nearest stock part to the 195 pF a 1.2 kHz target needed
distractors: It puts the corner at exactly 150 Hz, the band edge
It cancels the A3 gain-bandwidth pole at 609 kHz
It matches the stray capacitance at the stage-1 nodes
questions.explanation: The corner must be above 412 Hz for the phase spec and low enough to limit noise bandwidth (ENBW = π/2 × 1054 = 1656 Hz). 297 pF would give 788 Hz and 10.8°.
questions.modelAnswer: The 12 Oct design targeted 1.2 kHz (195 pF ideal); 222 pF was the nearest stock part, giving 1054 Hz and 8.1° of lag at 150 Hz.

questions.prompt: How much phase and gain does the low-pass cost at 150 Hz?
questions.correct: 8.1° of lag, 0.09 dB of droop
distractors: 45° of lag, 3 dB of droop
0.81° of lag, 0.01 dB of droop
20° of lag, 1 dB of droop
questions.explanation: A single pole lags by arctan(f/f_c) and droops by 10log(1 + (f/f_c)²). With f/f_c = 0.142 that is 8.1° and 0.09 dB.
questions.modelAnswer: arctan(150/1054) = 8.1° of lag and about 0.09 dB of droop.

questions.prompt: Why is there a 222 pF capacitor across R4_a (the reference leg) as well as across R4_b (the feedback)?
questions.correct: To keep both halves identical (Z4A = Z4B) at all frequencies
distractors: To make the low-pass second order, rolling off at 40 dB/decade
To decouple VREF to 0 V on the single supply
To stop A3 oscillating with 680 kΩ of feedback resistance
questions.explanation: A_c2 = (a − b)/(1 + a) with a and b the two arm ratios. If only one arm had C4, the ratios would differ above ~1 kHz and CMRR would collapse there. The filter is still first-order.
questions.modelAnswer: So both halves of the difference amplifier stay identical (Z4A = Z4B) at all frequencies; otherwise the ratios diverge with frequency and common-mode leaks through.

questions.prompt: What is A3's noise gain and closed-loop bandwidth?
distractors: G2 = 12.14, giving 8 MHz / 12.14 ≈ 659 kHz
G1·G2 = 130, giving 8 MHz / 130 ≈ 62 kHz
1, since A3 is a difference amp, giving 8 MHz
questions.explanation: For a difference amp the feedback factor is R3/(R3 + R4), so noise gain = 1 + R4/R3. That pole at 609 kHz is negligible.

questions.prompt: At 15 Hz what is the signal on A3's + pin?
questions.correct: ≈94 mV pk: 0.924 × V_O2 via the R3_a/R4_a divider
distractors: ≈2.47 V pk, the same as Vo, as A3 is a follower
≈102 mV pk, the full V_O2 with no divider
≈0 V, since A3's inputs form a virtual ground
questions.explanation: R3_a and R4_a form a divider from V_O2 to the reference. The − pin follows it, which is a quick check that A3 is in its linear range. It is not a virtual ground: only an inverting amp with the + pin grounded has that.

questions.prompt: What does matching between the A and B halves of stage 2 control?
questions.correct: The mid-band CMRR floor
distractors: The differential gain only
The low-pass corner only

questions.explanation: Input-referred: √2·i_n·R2/G1 = 174 nV/√Hz, R1 thermal 96 nV/√Hz, R2 thermal 31, sources 18, op-amp voltage noise 4.2. Total RSS 202.5 nV/√Hz.
questions.modelAnswer: The megohm resistors around stage 1: OP27 current noise flowing through R2, then R1 thermal noise.
questions.sayIt: The megohm resistors around stage 1 set the noise: OP27 current noise through R2 and thermal noise of R1.

questions.prompt: What is the noise bandwidth of the amplifier?
distractors: 1054 Hz, the −3 dB corner
150 Hz, the top of the spec band
609 kHz, A3's closed-loop bandwidth
questions.explanation: For a single-pole low-pass the equivalent noise bandwidth is π/2 × f_c.

questions.prompt: What output noise does the hand estimate give?
questions.correct: ≈1.1 mV rms, ≈7 mV p-p
distractors: ≈4.5 mV rms, ≈30 mV p-p
≈1.1 µV rms, ≈7 µV p-p
≈30 mV rms, ≈200 mV p-p
questions.explanation: v_rms = e_in·A_d·√ENBW = 202.5 n × 130 × 40.7 = 1.07 mV. Gaussian p-p ≈ 6.6 × rms.
questions.modelAnswer: About 1.1 mV rms (202.5 nV/√Hz × 130 × √1656), about 7 mV p-p.

questions.prompt: Why does the measured raw noise fail the 30 mV p-p limit?
questions.correct: 50 Hz pickup dominates; after a notch it is 15–18 mV p-p
distractors: OP27 current noise was underestimated by about a factor of ten
The 1054 Hz corner lets in far too much noise bandwidth
VREF's divider resistors add about 30 mV p-p of thermal noise
questions.explanation: Removing the 50 Hz part in quadrature leaves ~1.4 mV rms, close to the 1.1 mV estimate. The Brief (FAQ 6) allows a digital notch if PSD plots before and after are shown.
questions.modelAnswer: 50 Hz mains pickup dominates (3.1–3.4 mV rms of the 3.4–3.7 mV); after a 50 Hz notch it is 15–18 mV p-p.

questions.prompt: How is the noise test set up?
questions.correct: Inputs to the reference via 10 kΩ; max − min of Vo, Normal mode
distractors: Inputs left open-circuit; rms of Vo with the scope in High-Res mode
Inputs shorted together; Vo averaged over 64 frames, then p-p
1 Vpp common-mode applied; rms of Vo after a 50 Hz notch
questions.explanation: Averaging or High-Res hides noise. Records of 10 s, 1 s and 0.1 s, three each.
questions.modelAnswer: Generator off, each input to the reference through 10 kΩ, Vo captured in Normal acquisition; noise = max(Vo) − min(Vo).

questions.prompt: For Gaussian noise, roughly how many times the rms is the peak-to-peak?
questions.correct: About 6.6
distractors: Exactly 2
About 50 to 100
questions.explanation: 2.8 is for a sine wave. The 2 Nov records showed 50–100× the rms, which meant isolated spikes, not Gaussian noise.
questions.modelAnswer: About 6.6 (covering 99.9 % of peaks).

questions.prompt: What noise does the VREF network add?
questions.correct: ≈20 nV rms, negligible
distractors: ≈7.5 mV rms, a quarter of the limit
About the same as R1's thermal noise
Enough to double the output noise
questions.explanation: e_n = √(4kT·3.4 kΩ) = 7.5 nV/√Hz, filtered by C_ref to √(π/2 × 4.68 Hz). That is 0.13 µV p-p at the output.
questions.modelAnswer: About 20 nV rms (7.5 nV/√Hz in a 4.68 Hz bandwidth), negligible.

questions.prompt: The Lab 2 page gave 3.9 mV p-p noise. What did it leave out?
questions.correct: OP27 current noise flowing through R2
distractors: Thermal noise of R4 in stage 2
The 50 Hz mains component
Noise of the 10 kΩ source resistors
questions.explanation: That term is the biggest one. And 0.4 pA/√Hz is the 1 kHz figure; the datasheet gives 1.0 pA at 30 Hz and 1.7 pA at 10 Hz, so the real total is higher still.
questions.modelAnswer: The OP27 inverting-input current noise flowing through R2 (i_n × 3.3 MΩ = 1.3 µV/√Hz at each stage-1 output).

questions.prompt: How was the design converted to a single supply?
questions.correct: Two 6.8 kΩ + 10 µF make 7.5 V; signal returns go to it
distractors: Every 0 V node, op-amp pin 4 included, moves to VREF
A Zener and a buffer op-amp make a 7.5 V reference
The rail goes to 30 V and signal ground stays at 0 V
questions.explanation: R_ca, R_cb, the R4_a/C4_a leg, U2 pin 3 and the ECG divider shunt move to VREF. Pin 4 never goes to VREF. No extra chips (no buffer).
questions.modelAnswer: A 7.5 V mid-rail reference from two 6.8 kΩ resistors and 10 µF; every signal return that went to 0 V goes to VREF; op-amp pins go to 15 V and 0 V.
questions.sayIt: Two 6.8 k resistors and 10 microfarads make a 7.5 volt reference with 3.4 kΩ output resistance. Three returns move to it.

questions.prompt: Which of these does NOT move to VREF on the single supply?
questions.correct: Pin 4 (V−) of the OP27s
distractors: The bottom ends of R_ca and R_cb
The R4_a / C4_a reference leg
U2 pin 3 in the fixture
questions.explanation: Supply pins go to 15 V and 0 V. Pin 4 on VREF with an input near 0 V is what overheated U2 on 11 Nov.

questions.prompt: Why does the conversion work without redesigning the signal path?
questions.correct: The inputs are AC-coupled, and VREF is an AC ground like 0 V
distractors: The OP27 is rail-to-rail, so the output swing is unchanged
The gain was recalculated to fit the smaller single-supply swing
C_c doubles as the reference decoupling capacitor for VREF
questions.explanation: An AC signal only cares that the return node does not move. The transfer function is literally the same equation; the DC level everything rides on moves from 0 V to 7.5 V. The OP27 is not rail-to-rail (3 V output, 4 V input margins).
questions.modelAnswer: The inputs are AC-coupled, so nothing needs a DC path to the source, and every return sits at the same AC potential (held still by C_ref) as 0 V was.

questions.prompt: Why 15 V and not 30 V?
questions.correct: VREF must be 7.5 V; the generator's offset stops at 10 V
distractors: 15 V gives more output swing about VREF than 30 V would
The OP27 is rated for 15 V total supply at most
The 16 V capacitors would see the full 30 V rail and fail
questions.explanation: 30 V was also ruled out as too much for the parts. Half of 30 V is 15 V, beyond the generator's 10 V offset limit. C_ref sees only 7.5 V.
questions.modelAnswer: The fixture input must sit at VREF and the generator's DC offset stops at 10 V; 7.5 V is reachable, 15 V is not.
questions.sayIt: The fixture has to sit at VREF and the generator's DC offset stops at 10 V.

questions.prompt: What are VREF's value, Thévenin resistance and decoupling corner?
What is the output window and how much is spare for offset with a 20 mV QRS?
questions.correct: 3–12 V; 1.9 V spare
distractors: 0–15 V; 4.9 V spare
4–11 V; 0.9 V spare
questions.explanation: OP27 output guaranteed 3 V inside each rail (1.2 V typical). 4–11 V is the input window. With a 10 mV QRS, 3.2 V spare.
questions.modelAnswer: 3 V to 12 V (±4.5 V about VREF); 4.5 − 2.6 = 1.9 V spare.
questions.sayIt: 15 V rail, 7.5 V reference, 4–11 V input window, 3–12 V output window, 2.6 V signal, 1.9 V spare.

questions.prompt: What is the input common-mode window on the single supply and where do the + pins sit?
questions.correct: 4–11 V; pins at ≈7.43 V
distractors: 3–12 V; pins at 7.50 V exactly
0–15 V; pins at 0 V
4–11 V; pins at ≈0.68 V
questions.explanation: OP27 inputs stay 4 V inside each rail. 7.5 − 10 nA × 6.8 MΩ = 7.43 V typical (7.23 V at max I_b), more than 3 V clear either side.
questions.modelAnswer: 4 V to 11 V; the pins sit at about 7.43 V (VREF − I_b·R_c).

questions.prompt: Does the reference's 3.4 kΩ hurt CMRR?
questions.correct: Barely: ≈89 dB below 5 Hz, invisible in the data
distractors: Yes: it caps CMRR at 50 dB at all frequencies
Yes: it is the main limit above 20 Hz
No: it has no effect at any frequency
questions.modelAnswer: Barely: below 5 Hz it makes R4_a 0.5 % 'longer', limiting stage 2 to 68 dB, which stage 1 lifts to about 89 dB; not visible in the data.

questions.prompt: Why are wires fitted across the coupling capacitors at start-up?
questions.correct: To stop a 7.5 V step lifting the inputs to the rail
distractors: To discharge C_c so the patient never sees DC
To bypass the high-pass so DC gain can be read
To short the inputs together for the noise test
questions.explanation: The capacitor can hold a DC difference. With wires, both sides are one node, so nothing steps. VREF itself ramps in 0.17 s.
questions.modelAnswer: Without them the amplifier-side nodes spend ~52 s below the 4 V input floor, and when the generator's 7.5 V offset arrives the step passes through C_c and lifts the node to ~14.7 V, the supply rail.
questions.sayIt: They stop a 7.5 V step passing through the capacitors and lifting the inputs to the supply rail.

questions.prompt: Without the start-up wires, how long are the inputs below their 4 V floor?
distractors: τ = (R_c + R_s)C_c ≈ 68 s
5 × R_thC_ref = 5 × 34 ms ≈ 0.17 s
questions.explanation: The node charges as V_REF(1 − e^(−t/τ)) with τ = 68.1 s. 0.17 s is VREF's own settling.

questions.prompt: What is the correct power-on order?
questions.correct: Gen off, wires on, supply on, gen on, wait 5 s, wires off
distractors: Supply on, gen on, wait 300 s, then fit both wires
Wires on, gen on, supply on, then wires off straight away
Supply on, wires off, gen on, wait 5 s, then start the sweep
questions.explanation: Shut-down: fit both wires, generator off, supply off. With real electrodes the wires go from VREF to the amplifier side of each capacitor.
questions.modelAnswer: Generator output off, fit both wires, supply on, generator output on, wait 5 s, remove wires.

questions.prompt: Why must the generator's DC offset be set to VREF (≈7.5 V)?
questions.correct: U1's input must sit inside 4–11 V or the fixture saturates
distractors: It cancels the amplifier's own output DC offset at Vo
The coupling capacitors need 7.5 V across them to charge
It sets the fixture inverter's gain to exactly −1
questions.explanation: V2 − V1 = 2v(t) + 2(V_offset − V_REF). The differential signal is still 2v; the DC term is blocked by C_c and is near zero when V_offset = V_REF.
questions.modelAnswer: U1 buffers the generator, so its input must sit inside the 4–11 V window; at 0 V DC the fixture saturates (the 11 Nov failure).

questions.prompt: Why did U2 run hot on 11 Nov?
questions.correct: Pin 4 on VREF while its input sat at 0 V
distractors: Its output was driving C_ref directly
The supply had been set to 30 V
It was oscillating at about 1 kHz
questions.explanation: Lesson: pin 4 always to 0 V. Replace that chip.
questions.modelAnswer: Its pin 4 (V−) was on VREF while its pin 3 input was at 0 V, outside its supply range.

questions.prompt: Why do gain, corners, phase and CMRR not change on the single supply?
questions.correct: Same AC potential at every return; only DC levels move
distractors: The gain was recalculated for the 15 V rail to compensate
Because VREF is exactly 7.5 V, so no error can enter
They do change: about 4 dB of gain, as the logs show
questions.explanation: The lower supply changes open-loop gain by a negligible 0.0013 %. Same pole-zero diagrams for both builds. The logged 4 dB excess was a scope-resolution artefact on V2.
questions.modelAnswer: Every signal-path part keeps its value and returns to a node at the same AC potential; only DC levels move.

questions.prompt: The single-supply logs show 46 dB of gain. What is going on?
questions.correct: V2 was digitised in 8.44 mV steps, so it was under-read
distractors: The 3.4 kΩ reference impedance adds about 4 dB of gain
R3 was the wrong value on the single-supply board
The OP27 has more open-loop gain on 15 V, lifting the gain
questions.explanation: Do not quote 46 dB. Fix: read the scope in 16-bit mode or measure V2 another way. Phase survived because the fit locks onto the timing.
questions.modelAnswer: V2 (9.5 mV pk sitting on 7.5 V) was digitised in three 8.44 mV steps at 210 mV/div, so V2 was under-read; Vo itself matched ±15 V within 0.6 dB.

questions.prompt: How much 50 Hz supply ripple reaches VREF?
questions.correct: ≈0.047 of it, and it cancels when Vo is read against VREF
distractors: Half of it, since the divider is unfiltered at 50 Hz
None, because C_ref blocks 50 Hz completely
130 × the ripple, because it enters the signal path
questions.explanation: The divider halves it and C_ref low-passes it at 4.68 Hz.
questions.modelAnswer: 0.5/√(1 + (50/4.68)²) ≈ 0.047 of the ripple; it reaches Vo at gain 1 through the R4_a leg and cancels when Vo is read against VREF.

questions.prompt: Why wasn't a buffer op-amp added to drive VREF?
questions.correct: Stock parts only, and 3.4 kΩ costs just ≈89 dB of CMRR
distractors: A buffer would oscillate driving the 10 µF C_ref load
An OP27 cannot output 7.5 V from a 15 V rail
A buffer would add about 30 mV p-p of noise at the output
questions.explanation: A buffer would take the reference impedance to near zero, but it isn't needed.
questions.modelAnswer: No parts beyond the stock list, and the 3.4 kΩ reference impedance only costs about 89 dB of CMRR, far above the other limits.

questions.prompt: Why does the ECG divider's 1.2 kΩ shunt return to VREF on the single supply?
questions.correct: At 0 V the shunt would put U1's input at ≈0.68 V
distractors: It sets the divider ratio to exactly 1/11.04
It low-pass filters the synthetic ECG waveform
It turns the ECG into a common-mode test signal
questions.explanation: Same placement rule: anything that was a signal return goes to VREF. The divider ratio 1.2 k/(12 k + 1.2 k + 50 Ω) = 1/11.04.
questions.modelAnswer: With the shunt at 0 V, U1's input would sit at about 0.68 V, below its 4 V input floor.

questions.prompt: What is the 'placement rule' for every connection on the single supply?
questions.correct: Signal returns go to VREF; only supply pins and the divider touch 0 V
distractors: Every node that touched 0 V on ±15 V, pin 4 included, moves to VREF
Only the stage-2 parts move to VREF; stage 1 stays on 0 V
Every electrolytic capacitor's negative side is tied to 0 V
questions.explanation: Four kinds of node: floating between signal nodes (unchanged), signal returns (to VREF), supply pins (15 V / 0 V), the reference network (new).
questions.modelAnswer: Any return that carried the signal reference on ±15 V goes to VREF; only the op-amp supply pins and the reference divider touch 0 V.

questions.prompt: Which way round do the electrolytic capacitors go?
questions.correct: + side towards VREF / the amplifier side, 16 V
distractors: + side to 0 V, with a 16 V rating
Either way round, as 7.5 V is too little to matter
+ side to the 15 V rail, with a 25 V rating
questions.explanation: C_ref + to VREF. C_c + towards the amplifier. With real electrodes at 0 V, C_c sees up to 7.5 V, hence 16 V parts.
questions.modelAnswer: + side towards VREF / the amplifier side (higher DC potential); 16 V rating.

questions.prompt: Roughly how much current does the single-supply board draw?
questions.correct: About 11 mA
distractors: About 1.1 mA
About 110 mA
About 50 mA
questions.explanation: Divider 15 V/13.6 kΩ = 1.1 mA, 8.3 mW per resistor. OP27 ≈ 2 mA each at 15 V total.
questions.modelAnswer: About 11 mA (10 mA for five OP27s + 1.1 mA divider), 14 mA hot.

questions.prompt: What does the single supply cost compared with ±15 V?
questions.correct: Margin: 1.9 V offset room instead of 9.4 V, plus start-up care
distractors: About 6 dB of gain, because the supply has been halved
CMRR drops below 60 dB at low frequency from the VREF leg
The low-pass corner moves down to about 500 Hz
questions.explanation: Gain, corners, phase and A_c are unchanged (S9). The 13 Nov data agreed with ±15 V to 0.6 dB and 0.6°.
questions.modelAnswer: Margin, not performance: output headroom for offset falls from 9.4 V to 1.9 V, start-up needs a procedure, and the instruments struggle with mV signals on 7.5 V DC.
questions.sayIt: Headroom: Vo must stay between 3 V and 12 V, leaving 1.9 V for offset with a 20 mV QRS. And settling: the input capacitors charge to 7.5 V through 6.8 MΩ, 68 s.

questions.prompt: How is V_id obtained from the fixture?
questions.correct: V2 buffered, V1 = −V2 inverted, so V_id = 2V2
distractors: V_id = V2, the generator output passed straight through
V_id = V2 − VREF on the single supply only
V_id = V2/2, because it is split across the two inputs
questions.explanation: Matched 10 kΩ in U2 give exactly −1. On one supply U2 inverts about VREF.
questions.modelAnswer: U1 buffers the generator (V2) and U2 inverts it (V1 = −V2), so V_id = 2 × V2.

questions.prompt: Why must the fixture inverter's two 10 kΩ resistors match?
questions.correct: A mismatch makes V1 ≠ −V2, adding common-mode
distractors: They set the 10 kΩ electrode source impedance
They match the electrode impedance for power
They set the amplifier's differential gain
questions.explanation: The test signal should be purely differential. A mismatch makes the gain measurement depend on CMRR.
questions.modelAnswer: Unequal resistors make V1 ≠ −V2, adding a common-mode component to the test signal.

questions.prompt: Why is the scope DC-coupled for gain and phase?
questions.correct: Scope AC coupling adds its own high-pass lead
distractors: AC coupling would only block the 7.5 V offset
DC coupling has a lower noise floor
The Brief requires DC coupling for CMRR only
questions.explanation: The scope's AC coupling corner (~Hz) would distort the 0.5 Hz phase.
questions.modelAnswer: AC coupling adds its own high-pass, which adds phase lead at low frequency.

questions.prompt: What do the 10 kΩ source resistors represent, and when are they removed?
questions.correct: Electrode impedance; removed for the CMRR test
distractors: Op-amp current limiting; never removed
The input bias path; removed for the noise test
Part of the gain network; removed for phase
questions.explanation: For noise they stay (inputs to the reference through 10 kΩ).
questions.modelAnswer: The electrode impedance (Brief: 10 kΩ ±10 %); removed for the CMRR test, as the Brief's set-up shows.

questions.prompt: On 19 Oct CMRR was flat at about 44 dB and phase was −10.5° at 1 kHz. What was wrong?
questions.correct: C4 missing or open; flat A_c means a difference-stage fault
distractors: The coupling capacitors were fitted the wrong way round
Input time constants mismatched by about 20 %
Stray capacitance at the 3.3 MΩ stage-1 inverting nodes
questions.explanation: With 1054 Hz roll-off, phase at 1 kHz should be about −43°. −10.5° meant no roll-off. Flat CMRR = resistor/difference-stage problem.
questions.modelAnswer: C4 was missing or open, and a flat A_c pointed to an imbalance in the difference stage.

questions.prompt: Why did V_cm read 0.5–0.9 Vpp when 1 Vpp was applied (19 Oct)?
questions.correct: Averaged captures with Auto trigger misaligned frames
distractors: The generator was left in 50 Ω mode, halving V_cm
The scope probe was set to ×10 instead of ×1
The coupling capacitors attenuated V_cm at low frequency
questions.explanation: Fix: Normal trigger for averaged captures.
questions.modelAnswer: Averaged captures were taken with Auto trigger, so misaligned frames were averaged.

questions.prompt: Why did the ECG tests come out twice the intended size on 2 Nov?
questions.correct: The generator stretches waveforms and has a 20 mVpp floor
distractors: The ECG file was sampled at twice the playback rate
The amplifier gain was 260, not 130
The ECG divider was fitted the wrong way round
questions.explanation: Fix: a 12 kΩ / 1.2 kΩ divider (÷11.04) in front of U1. Run 1 assumed a 1 kΩ shunt and was 1.18× too large.
questions.modelAnswer: The 33220A stretches an arbitrary waveform to its amplitude setting and cannot go below 20 mVpp into High-Z.

questions.prompt: What does PRD measure in the ECG test?
questions.correct: RMS difference between output (÷ gain) and a reference, in %
distractors: Ratio of QRS peak to P-wave peak at the output, in %
Phase response deviation at 150 Hz relative to 15 Hz, in %
Power-supply rejection of the board at 50 Hz, in %
questions.explanation: PRD = 100√(Σ(y − x)²/Σx²). 'In to out' uses the measured input; 'vs clean' uses the noise-free ECG, so tests with deliberate wander or EMG look worse on that column.
questions.modelAnswer: Percentage root-mean-square difference between the output (scaled back by the gain) and a reference waveform.

questions.prompt: In the CMRR script, what happens if phase_results.csv is missing?
questions.correct: It falls back to a nominal 42.3 dB A_d
distractors: It refuses to run and raises an error
It measures A_d itself from the CMRR data
It assumes 60 dB CMRR for every point
questions.explanation: Lesson: run the phase sweep first, in the same folder.
questions.modelAnswer: It falls back to a nominal 42.3 dB for A_d, so the CMRR file shows A_d as a flat 42.3 dB.

questions.prompt: What would you improve given more time?
questions.correct: Better V2 resolution, 150 Hz CMRR, 50 Hz shielding, symmetric wiring
distractors: Raise the gain to 500 to fill the 3–12 V output window
Move the corners to exactly 0.5 Hz and 150 Hz to cut noise
Swap to rail-to-rail op-amps and go back to the ±15 V build
questions.explanation: Each item traces back to a measured weakness: the 46 dB artefact, the missing 150 Hz CMRR point, raw noise failing on 50 Hz, and the stray-C slope.
questions.modelAnswer: Read V2 at higher resolution on the single supply, measure CMRR at 150 Hz, shield against 50 Hz, and symmetrise the stage-1 wiring to cut the stray-capacitance term.

questions.prompt: Why does the 2 Nov noise record (216–516 mV p-p) not reflect the amplifier?
questions.correct: Isolated spikes: p-p was 50–100× an rms of only ≈4 mV
distractors: The amplifier was oscillating at high frequency during capture
The low-pass capacitor C4 was missing, so bandwidth was huge
The test was accidentally run with 1 Vpp common-mode applied
questions.explanation: Gaussian noise gives ~6.6× rms. Honest statement: those records fail and were not repeated on ±15 V.
questions.modelAnswer: The p-p was 50–100× the rms (rms only ~4 mV), so it captured isolated spikes of interference; they were absent from the 13 Nov records.

questions.prompt: Why must the generator's 50 Ω / High-Z setting be checked?
questions.correct: It changes the real amplitude by a factor of two
distractors: It changes the output frequency by a factor of two
It sets the range of DC offset the generator can add
It shifts the output phase by 90°
questions.explanation: The generator assumes a 50 Ω load in 50 Ω mode; into the high-impedance fixture the real amplitude is double what is displayed.

questions.prompt: Simulated CMRR in LTspice with ideal matched parts comes out far above the bench. Why?
questions.correct: Perfectly matched parts and no stray C in the simulation
distractors: LTspice's OP27 model has better CMRR than real parts
The bench scope injects extra common-mode
LTspice ignores the coupling capacitors
questions.explanation: With matched parts the single-supply sim showed ~87 dB below 1 Hz (from the 3.4 kΩ reference leg) rising to ~117 dB at 150 Hz.
questions.modelAnswer: The simulation has perfectly matched resistors and capacitors and no stray capacitance; a 1 % mismatch or Monte Carlo run makes it comparable.

questions.prompt: How is noise measured against the single supply's VREF on long records, and why?
questions.correct: Against VREF, because of sub-hertz VREF drift and settling
distractors: Against 0 V, because VREF itself carries too much noise
Against the 15 V rail, since that is the supply return
It makes no difference which node is used for a noise record
questions.explanation: 10 s records gave 58–146 mV. Settle longer and measure Vo − VREF.
questions.modelAnswer: Vo should be read against VREF, because 10 s records showed sub-hertz wander from capacitors still charging or VREF drift read against 0 V.

questions.prompt: What if R3 were 51 kΩ instead of 56 kΩ? What would the mid-band differential gain be (ignore the 0.15 % input loss)?
questions.explanation: G2 = R4/R3 = 680/51 = 13.3. Total = G1 × G2 = 10.71 × 13.3 = 143 → 43.1 dB. Distractors: G2 alone, using 1 + R4/R3 (that's A3's noise gain), or the as-built 130.

questions.prompt: What if R3 were 75 kΩ instead of 56 kΩ? What would the mid-band differential gain be (ignore the 0.15 % input loss)?
questions.explanation: G2 = R4/R3 = 680/75 = 9.07. Total = G1 × G2 = 10.71 × 9.07 = 97.1 → 39.7 dB. Distractors: G2 alone, using 1 + R4/R3 (that's A3's noise gain), or the as-built 130.

questions.prompt: What if R3 were 62 kΩ instead of 56 kΩ? What would the mid-band differential gain be (ignore the 0.15 % input loss)?
questions.explanation: G2 = R4/R3 = 680/62 = 11.0. Total = G1 × G2 = 10.71 × 11.0 = 117 → 41.4 dB. Distractors: G2 alone, using 1 + R4/R3 (that's A3's noise gain), or the as-built 130.

questions.prompt: What if R3 were 39 kΩ instead of 56 kΩ? What would the mid-band differential gain be (ignore the 0.15 % input loss)?
questions.explanation: G2 = R4/R3 = 680/39 = 17.4. Total = G1 × G2 = 10.71 × 17.4 = 187 → 45.4 dB. Distractors: G2 alone, using 1 + R4/R3 (that's A3's noise gain), or the as-built 130.

questions.prompt: What if R3 were 47 kΩ instead of 56 kΩ? What would the mid-band differential gain be (ignore the 0.15 % input loss)?
questions.explanation: G2 = R4/R3 = 680/47 = 14.5. Total = G1 × G2 = 10.71 × 14.5 = 155 → 43.8 dB. Distractors: G2 alone, using 1 + R4/R3 (that's A3's noise gain), or the as-built 130.

questions.prompt: What if R3 were 43 kΩ instead of 56 kΩ? What would the mid-band differential gain be (ignore the 0.15 % input loss)?
questions.explanation: G2 = R4/R3 = 680/43 = 15.8. Total = G1 × G2 = 10.71 × 15.8 = 169 → 44.6 dB. Distractors: G2 alone, using 1 + R4/R3 (that's A3's noise gain), or the as-built 130.

questions.prompt: What if C4 were 470 pF (with R4 = 680 kΩ)? Where is the low-pass corner, and how much lag does it add at 150 Hz?
questions.correct: 498 Hz, 17° lag at 150 Hz
distractors: 6.05 kHz, 1.4° lag at 150 Hz
3.13 kHz, 2.7° lag at 150 Hz
498 Hz, 73° lag at 150 Hz
questions.explanation: f = 1/(2π R4 C4) = 1/(2π × 680 kΩ × 470 pF) = 498 Hz. Lag = arctan(150/498) = 17°. Still inside the 20° limit. Common slips: using R3, dropping the 2π (that gives rad/s), or inverting the arctan ratio.

questions.prompt: What if C4 were 180 pF (with R4 = 680 kΩ)? Where is the low-pass corner, and how much lag does it add at 150 Hz?
questions.correct: 1.30 kHz, 6.6° lag at 150 Hz
distractors: 15.8 kHz, 0.54° lag at 150 Hz
